solutions.check: grid and clues read from the FT's printable PDF, its numbering matching the clue list; every fifteensquared answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Members of brotherhood out to get Hitler-appeaser

indicators.note: out here means put out of order, so the letters of the compound word are rearranged

explanation.surface: Some members of a fraternity are out to get a politician who appeased Hitler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges HITLER-APPEASER, all fourteen letters. The Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood was a group of Victorian English painters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pre-Raphaelites were the painters and poets who formed the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood in 1848.

clue.text: Course offering education in various faiths to new student

parts.note: RE is religious education, the school subject covering the world's faiths
a fresher is a first-year university student in Britain

explanation.surface: A course on world religions is offered to a first-year student.
explanation.walkthrough: RE (religious education) is a standard British school subject.
explanation.definitionFit: A refresher is a short training course that brings existing skills up to date.

clue.text: Once a cold drink with explosive content

indicators.note: content means contents here, so the explosive is what the drink holds inside it

parts.note: rum is an alcoholic drink
HE stands for high explosive

explanation.surface: Someone is offered a dangerous cocktail with something explosive inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Rheum is an old word for a cold or catarrh, a watery discharge from the nose.

clue.text: Father in capital city wants us brought up together

indicators.note: in places the father inside the name of the capital city

parts.note: Paris is the capital of France
pa is an informal word for father

indicators.note: in a down clue, brought up means the word us is written from bottom to top

explanation.surface: A father living in the capital wants his family moved up there together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought up' reverses the pronoun; in a down answer that turned piece sits at the bottom. Pari passu is a legal and financial phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Pari passu is Latin for 'with equal step', meaning side by side or at the same rate, so together.

clue.text: Sort of book finally falling short

indicators.note: falling short means the phrase stops before its last letter

parts.note: finally means at last

explanation.surface: Some sort of book arrives at last but falls short of expectations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'falling short' cuts the final T from AT LAST.
explanation.definitionFit: An atlas is a book of maps, a particular kind of book.

clue.text: Appealing frantically for a small donation

indicators.note: frantically suggests wild disorder, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone appeals frantically for a small gift of money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'frantically' rearranges APPEALING.
explanation.definitionFit: A lagniappe is a small extra gift given free, as a bonus a shopkeeper gives with a purchase.

clue.text: Hawk crossing river finds fish

indicators.note: crossing means the first word spans the second, which sits inside it

parts.note: to hawk is to sell aggressively, which is what a tout does

explanation.surface: A bird of prey flying over a river spots a fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hawk' looks like the bird, but it is the verb meaning to peddle.
explanation.definitionFit: Trout is a kind of freshwater fish of the salmon family.

clue.text: Reckon first half of game's watchers will include you and me

indicators.note: will include means the shortened word holds the pronoun inside it
first half of keeps only the opening five of the ten letters

parts.note: the people watching a game are spectators
you and me together are us

explanation.surface: Someone reckons the crowd at a match will include the two of us.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first half of' applies to the synonym, not the clue words, and 'will include' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: To suspect something is to think or reckon it is so, without proof.

clue.text: Jazz and art in France will give some folk a living

parts.note: trad is traditional jazz
in French, tu es means you are, the old English 'thou art'

explanation.surface: Playing jazz and art in France provides some people with a living.
explanation.walkthrough: 'art' is the old form of 'are', not painting: French 'es' is the same verb form.
explanation.definitionFit: Trades are skilled occupations, the work by which people earn a living.

clue.text: One has no time for toy gun

indicators.note: has no means a letter is taken away from the word

parts.note: to toy with something is to trifle with it

explanation.surface: A child gives up wasting time on a toy gun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'toy' is the verb, to trifle; drop T from TRIFLE.
explanation.definitionFit: A rifle is a long-barrelled firearm, a type of gun.

clue.text: Fussy girlies mingling outside old university

indicators.note: outside means the rearranged letters wrap around the university abbreviation
mingling means mixing together, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: OU is short for the Open University, or Oxford University

explanation.surface: Fussy young women mingle outside an old university.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fussy' looks like it describes the girlies, but it is the definition: religious can mean meticulous. 'mingling' signals the anagram and 'outside' the container.
explanation.definitionFit: Religious can mean scrupulous or punctilious, as in religious attention to detail, which is fussy behaviour.

clue.text: Concoct drug-containing spirit at Oxford?

indicators.note: containing means the spirit holds the drug inside it

parts.note: a dram is a measure of spirit, especially whisky
E is ecstasy, the drug
a student at university, Oxford above all, is said to be up

explanation.surface: Someone at Oxford invents a drink spiked with drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' is the old British usage for being in residence at a university.
explanation.definitionFit: To dream up is an idiom for inventing or devising something, so concoct.

clue.text: Prime bits from that lovely entertainer associated with satire — one gets bowled over

indicators.note: associated with links the two pieces, letting the satire word stand first in the answer

parts.note: a skit is a short satirical sketch

indicators.note: prime bits are the first letters of each of the next three words

explanation.surface: A lovely comic entertainer is linked with satire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'associated with' lets SKIT go before the three first letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A skittle is a pin knocked down by a bowled ball, so it gets bowled over.

clue.text: Term of respect — it comes with greeting to British

parts.note: it means sex appeal, SA
hi is a greeting

explanation.surface: A respectful term arrives along with a hello to the British.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it' meaning sex appeal (SA) is an old crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: Sahib was a respectful form of address for a man in colonial India, like sir.

clue.text: Youngster growing up can always become an adventurer

indicators.note: in a down clue, growing up means the word is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a cub is a young animal, or a junior scout
taken as written
e'er is the poetic short form of ever, always

explanation.surface: A child growing up can always turn into an adventurer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'growing up' turns CUB into BUC.
explanation.definitionFit: A buccaneer was a pirate, and is used for any reckless adventurer.

clue.text: One's most drowsy in wet weather after eating pasties?

indicators.note: after eating means the weather word holds the food inside it

parts.note: sleet is wet, icy weather
pasties are pies, pastry cases filled with meat or vegetables

explanation.surface: Someone becomes very drowsy outside in the rain after eating pasties.
explanation.walkthrough: A pasty is a Cornish pastry with a filling, a kind of pie.
explanation.definitionFit: Sleepiest is the superlative of sleepy, meaning most drowsy.

clue.text: Being unable to reach maturity could make one pine maybe

definitions.meaning: staying green for ever, never ripening
a pine keeps its needles all year round

explanation.surface: Someone who never grows up could become one who pines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pine' looks like a verb meaning yearn, but it is the tree.
explanation.definitionFit: Something forever green has never ripened, and a pine is a tree that keeps its leaves all year.

clue.text: Grand part of hospital about to become a very disturbed place

parts.note: epic means grand in scale
ENT is the ear, nose and throat department
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: A grand hospital department is about to become chaotic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' is RE, not a sign to move letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An epicentre is the point on the surface directly above an earthquake's origin, where the ground is shaken hardest.

clue.text: Building — one for the university gets such a condemnation

indicators.note: for means one letter is put in place of the other

parts.note: a structure is a building
U is the abbreviation for university
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A university building is condemned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one for the university' replaces U with I in STRUCTURE.
explanation.definitionFit: A stricture is a severe criticism, a censure or condemnation.

clue.text: Trudge under the sun — looking forward to this?

indicators.note: in a down clue, under means the trudge word goes beneath the sun abbreviation

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for sun or Sunday
to lumber is to move heavily, to trudge

explanation.surface: After a long trudge in the heat someone looks forward to a rest.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the tired walker's thought: sleep is what they long for.
explanation.definitionFit: A weary trudger would look forward to slumber, a deep sleep, so it fits as the question's answer.

clue.text: English winner denied the gold is put out

indicators.note: denied means the winner word loses some of its letters

parts.note: a victor is a winner
or is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: An English winner stripped of his gold medal is expelled.
explanation.walkthrough: OR for gold comes from heraldry.
explanation.definitionFit: To evict is to put out a tenant from a property.

clue.text: Duck eating the outside bits of some plant

indicators.note: eating means the duck takes the letters inside itself

parts.note: a teal is a small duck

indicators.note: the outside bits are the first and last letters of the next word

explanation.surface: A duck nibbles the outer leaves of some plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Teasel is a prickly plant whose dried heads were used to raise the nap on cloth.

clue.text: Removes a French food when seconds have been swallowed

indicators.note: have been swallowed means the letter goes inside the other words

parts.note: un is French for a
eats is slang for food

explanation.surface: Someone clears away a French meal after second helpings have been eaten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seconds' looks like second helpings, but it is the time unit S.
explanation.definitionFit: To unseat is to remove someone from a seat or a position of power.

clue.text: Smart piece of deception

definitions.meaning: to smart is to hurt with a sharp pain
a con trick, an elaborate swindle or police set-up

explanation.definitionFit: A sting is a sharp pain, as is to smart, and also slang for an elaborate confidence trick.

clue.text: Opening test coming up in South Africa

indicators.note: in puts the turned test inside the country abbreviation

parts.note: SA is South Africa

indicators.note: in a down clue, coming up means the word is written from bottom to top

parts.note: the MOT is the annual British roadworthiness test for vehicles

explanation.surface: An examination is about to take place in South Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming up' turns MOT into TOM.
explanation.definitionFit: A stoma is a small opening, such as a pore in a leaf or a surgical opening.

clue.text: Queen in the country with time to see something in the garden

indicators.note: in places the queen inside the country abbreviation

parts.note: GB is Great Britain
ER stands for Elizabeth Regina
an era is a period of time

explanation.surface: The queen spends time in the country visiting a garden.
explanation.definitionFit: A gerbera is a daisy-like flowering plant grown in gardens.

clue.text: Puzzle regarding alternative to the car

parts.note: re means regarding
a bus is another way to travel instead of by car

explanation.surface: A puzzle about choosing public transport over driving.
explanation.definitionFit: A rebus is a puzzle in which pictures or symbols stand for words or syllables.

clue.text: Old man about to get involved in bung, one anticipating a successful match

indicators.note: involved in means put inside the bribe word

parts.note: a bung is British slang for a bribe

indicators.note: about means the pair of pieces is turned round

parts.note: Ted is a typical man's name

explanation.surface: An old man is about to be caught up in a bribery case, hoping to fix a match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' turns OTED into DETO, which goes inside BRIBE.
explanation.definitionFit: A bride-to-be is engaged and anticipating marriage, a successful match of a different sort.

clue.text: Clean energy supplied to West Country city

indicators.note: supplied to means the energy is added after the city name

parts.note: Bath is a city in Somerset, in south-west England
E is the symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Green energy is supplied to a city in the West Country.
explanation.walkthrough: The West Country is south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: To bathe is to wash, to clean in water.

clue.text: I ran, drunk with strong beer? Surely not!

definitions.text: I ran, drunk with strong beer? Surely not!

indicators.note: drunk means intoxicated, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A runner claims to have run while drunk on strong beer, which is unbelievable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drunk' rearranges I RAN and STRONG BEER. Roger Bannister ran the first sub-four-minute mile in 1954, hardly on beer.
explanation.definitionFit: Roger Bannister was the English athlete who first ran a mile in under four minutes, so he could say he ran.
